title: If you're looking, here's a "good deal" for NASA and the European Space Agency
gist: NASA under Jared Isaacman is demanding 'good deals' from international partners amid a Moon Base and China-race focus, creating friction with ESA after cancellation of Gateway and Mars Sample Return. The LISA gravitational wave mission is held up as a good deal, but White House budget proposals to cancel it, Envision and others leave the future of joint missions uncertain.

insights.claim: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman says international partners must make meaningful contributions with greater urgency, offering something NASA or US companies are not already doing and delivering when NASA needs it.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Partnership terms are tightening; partners need differentiated contributions.

insights.claim: NASA canceled the Lunar Gateway and Mars Sample Return (whose budget ballooned beyond $10 billion) as it prioritizes a south pole Moon Base and competition with China, leaving lesser priorities behind without a major budget increase.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Human spaceflight and Moon Base spending crowd out robotic science; beneficiaries are lunar surface contractors.

insights.claim: Isaacman dismissed an ESA proposal for a European cargo lander for the Moon Base, a role NASA expects US-built landers to fill; he cited Japan's pressurized rover and Italy's first Moon Base habitat as good deals.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: US commercial landers favored over European; Japanese and Italian contributions are examples of what gets accepted.

insights.claim: LISA is a European-led gravitational wave observatory with three spacecraft 2.5 million km apart, launching around 2035, with NASA supplying laser transmitters and telescopes, charge management devices and data analysis support while Europe builds, launches and operates.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Defines split of responsibilities for a flagship science mission.

insights.claim: NASA's Ira Thorpe says the US pays roughly a third of LISA but receives all the science data, versus about $3 billion if the US did it alone; NASA's work is expected to cost around $1 billion with no firm budget commitment.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Cost leverage explains why LISA is considered a model good deal.
insights.quote: We are paying for roughly a third [of the mission]

insights.claim: ESA approved LISA in 2024 with a budget of 1.75 billion euros ($2 billion), excluding US and member state contributions.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark

insights.claim: The White House proposed canceling NASA's LISA participation last year and again in its 2027 request, but Congress rejected the cuts and funded it in FY2026 with a specific line in the appropriations bill.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Congress is a backstop against White House science cuts; watch FY2027 appropriations.

insights.claim: Sen. Chris Van Hollen and Rep. Glenn Ivey, whose Maryland constituencies include Goddard Space Flight Center, sit on the NASA appropriations subcommittees, and Van Hollen could chair his if Democrats win the Senate in the midterms.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Midterm control of the Senate could shift NASA science funding.

insights.claim: NASA's astrophysics head Shawn Domagal-Goldman said NASA will maintain its LISA commitment as long as funding stays at FY26 levels, including under a continuing resolution.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Continuing resolution risk is covered for LISA.

insights.claim: NASA has booked a SpaceX launch in 2028 for ESA's Rosalind Franklin Mars rover, which is currently the only future Mars rover with NASA involvement, after Congress funded it despite administration attempts to cancel.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: SpaceX gains a launch contract tied to congressional funding.

insights.claim: NASA's role in New Athena is described as fully committed but without a specific congressional funding callout, and the US role in ESA's Envision Venus mission looks unlikely as ESA contracts a European radar instrument instead of one from JPL.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Europe is preparing to go it alone on missions where NASA support wavers.
